claim: MFSD1 is a member of the major facilitator superfamily.
source: MFSD1 is a poorly characterized protein. It belongs to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) of transporters, one of the two largest family of transporter proteins mediating secondary active or passive transport processes over cellular membranes (Pao et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states MFSD1 belongs to the MFS family and cites Pao et al., 1998.

claim: MFSD1 is co-expressed in the TFEB-mediated gene network regulating lysosomal biogenesis.
source: MFSD1 is co-expressed in the transcription factor EB (TFEB)-mediated gene network regulating lysosomal biogenesis and lysosomal gene expression and was thus identified as a direct TFEB-target gene (Palmieri et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites Palmieri et al., 2011 as evidence for MFSD1 being a TFEB target gene.

claim: Overexpression of epitope-tagged MFSD1 shows co-localization with LAMP-proteins.
source: Overexpression of epitope-tagged MFSD1 indicated co-localization with LAMP-proteins, demonstrating that it is indeed a resident lysosomal protein (Chapel et al., 2013; Palmieri et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites Chapel et al., 2013 and Palmieri et al., 2011 as evidence for MFSD1 co-localization with LAMP proteins.

claim: MFSD1 localizes to the plasma membrane of neurons.
source: However, there are also reports showing non-lysosomal localization of MFSD1 at the plasma membrane of neurons and the Golgi-apparatus (Perland et al., 2017; Valoskova et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Perland et al., 2017 and Valoskova et al., 2019 as evidence for non-lysosomal localization.

claim: MFSD1 localizes to the Golgi apparatus.
source: However, there are also reports showing non-lysosomal localization of MFSD1 at the plasma membrane of neurons and the Golgi-apparatus (Perland et al., 2017; Valoskova et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites Perland et al., 2017 and Valoskova et al., 2019 as evidence for Golgi localization.

claim: Endogenous MFSD1 is localized in lysosomes.
source: Endogenous MFSD1 is localized in lysosomes.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript summary section.

claim: MFSD1 harbors a dileucine-based sorting motif in its cytosolic N-terminus.
source: It harbors a dileucine-based sorting motif in its cytosolic N-terminus which is required for its transport to lysosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and supported by experimental data showing mislocalization of mutants.

claim: The dileucine-based sorting motif is required for MFSD1 transport to lysosomes.
source: It harbors a dileucine-based sorting motif in its cytosolic N-terminus which is required for its transport to lysosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and supported by experimental data in Figure 1I-J.

claim: MFSD1-deficient mice develop a severe liver disease.
source: MFSD1-deficient mice develop a severe liver disease characterized by extravasation of erythrocytes, sinusoidal damage, loss of liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) and finally signs of fibrosis.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and supported by histological and biochemical data in Figure 2.

claim: MFSD1-deficient mice show extravasation of erythrocytes in the liver.
source: MFSD1-deficient mice develop a severe liver disease characterized by extravasation of erythrocytes, sinusoidal damage, loss of liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) and finally signs of fibrosis.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and supported by histological data in Figure 2H-I.

claim: MFSD1-deficient mice show sinusoidal damage in the liver.
source: MFSD1-deficient mice develop a severe liver disease characterized by extravasation of erythrocytes, sinusoidal damage, loss of liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) and finally signs of fibrosis.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and supported by histological data in Figure 2H-I.

claim: MFSD1-deficient mice show loss of liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs).
source: MFSD1-deficient mice develop a severe liver disease characterized by extravasation of erythrocytes, sinusoidal damage, loss of liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) and finally signs of fibrosis.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and supported by histological data in Figure 2H-I.

claim: MFSD1-deficient mice show signs of fibrosis in the liver.
source: MFSD1-deficient mice develop a severe liver disease characterized by extravasation of erythrocytes, sinusoidal damage, loss of liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) and finally signs of fibrosis.
evidence: This is stated in the manuscript and supported by Sirius Red staining in Figure 2H.

claim: GLMP is a critical accessory subunit for MFSD1.
source: Proteomics of isolated lysosomes from Mfsd1 knockout mice revealed GLMP as a critical accessory subunit for MFSD1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by proteomics data in Figure 3.

claim: MFSD1 and GLMP physically interact.
source: MFSD1 and GLMP physically interact.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5A.

claim: GLMP is essential for the maintenance of normal levels of MFSD1 in lysosomes.
source: GLMP is essential for the maintenance of normal levels of MFSD1 in lysosomes and vice versa.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4A.

claim: MFSD1 is essential for the maintenance of normal levels of GLMP in lysosomes.
source: GLMP is essential for the maintenance of normal levels of MFSD1 in lysosomes and vice versa.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Glmp knockout mice mimic the phenotype of Mfsd1 knockout mice.
source: Glmp knockout mice mimic the phenotype of Mfsd1 knockout mice.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by histological and molecular data in Figure 4.

claim: N- and C-terminally HA-tagged MFSD1 co-localizes with LAMP2 in HeLa cells.
source: Co-immunofluorescence staining with antibodies against HA, LAMP2 and MFSD1 confirmed the co-localization of MFSD1 (either detected with HA- or MFSD1 antibodies) with LAMP2 and the specificity of our MFSD1 antibody.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: HA-tagged MFSD1 shows a major band of approximately 35 kDa by immunoblot.
source: By immunoblot, both HA- and MFSD1-antibodies detected a major band of ~35 kDa for N- or C-terminally tagged MFSD1 in transfected cells, differing from the predicted molecular weight of ~51 kDa (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The predicted molecular weight of MFSD1 is approximately 51 kDa.
source: By immunoblot, both HA- and MFSD1-antibodies detected a major band of ~35 kDa for N- or C-terminally tagged MFSD1 in transfected cells, differing from the predicted molecular weight of ~51 kDa (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Endogenous MFSD1 is enriched in magnetite-bead isolated lysosomes from MEFs.
source: These data were corroborated by analyzing magnetite-bead isolated lysosomes compared to the postnuclear supernatant from MEFs, showing a pronounced enrichment of endogenous MFSD1 in the lysosome-enriched fraction similar to the striking enrichment of the lysosome-marker LAMP1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: MFSD1 is detected ubiquitously in murine organs with highest levels in kidney and spleen.
source: We next investigated the tissue-specific expression of MFSD1 using our antibody (Figure 1E). MFSD1 was detected ubiquitously in murine organs and highest levels were observed in kidney and spleen.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MFSD1 has 12 transmembrane domains with both N- and C-termini in the cytosol.
source: These experiments clearly revealed that MFSD1 presents with an even number of TMDs and likely a 12 TMD spanning topology (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by selective permeabilization experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MFSD1 contains a dileucine-based sorting motif (EDRALL, amino acids 7-12) in its N-terminus.
source: We identified a dileucine-based lysosomal sorting motif close to the cytosolic N-terminus of murine MFSD1 (amino acid 7–12, EDRALL) that is highly conserved among different species and bears similarity to motifs found in MFSD8 and SLC17A5/Sialin, structurally related lysosomal transporters (Figure 1F,G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1F-H.

claim: The dileucine motif in MFSD1 is highly conserved among different species.
source: We identified a dileucine-based lysosomal sorting motif close to the cytosolic N-terminus of murine MFSD1 (amino acid 7–12, EDRALL) that is highly conserved among different species and bears similarity to motifs found in MFSD8 and SLC17A5/Sialin, structurally related lysosomal transporters (Figure 1F,G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Approximately 2% of cells transfected with wildtype MFSD1 with an internal HA-tag show MFSD1 at the plasma membrane.
source: While only subtle amounts of wildtype-MFSD1 with the internal HA-tag were detectable at the PM after transfection of Hela cells and staining for HA (~2% of the cells), a considerably higher number of MFSD1-positive cells was observed after transfection with MFSD1LL/AA (~20% of the cells) (Figure 1J (II-III)).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Approximately 20% of cells transfected with MFSD1LL/AA with an internal HA-tag show MFSD1 at the plasma membrane.
source: While only subtle amounts of wildtype-MFSD1 with the internal HA-tag were detectable at the PM after transfection of Hela cells and staining for HA (~2% of the cells), a considerably higher number of MFSD1-positive cells was observed after transfection with MFSD1LL/AA (~20% of the cells) (Figure 1J (II-III)).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1J.

claim: MFSD1 is not N-glycosylated.
source: However, none of the two endoglycosidases altered the apparent molecular weight of MFSD1, indicating a lack of N-glycosylation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by deglycosylation experiments in Figure 1K-L.

claim: MFSD1 contains two putative N-glycosylation sites (N76 and N449).
source: MFSD1 contains two putative N-glycosylation sites (N76 and N449).
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: Treatment with PNGaseF does not alter the apparent molecular weight of MFSD1.
source: However, none of the two endoglycosidases altered the apparent molecular weight of MFSD1, indicating a lack of N-glycosylation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Treatment with Endoglycosidase H does not alter the apparent molecular weight of MFSD1.
source: However, none of the two endoglycosidases altered the apparent molecular weight of MFSD1, indicating a lack of N-glycosylation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1K.

claim: No differences in weight gain are observed between wildtype and Mfsd1 KO mice until 13 weeks of age.
source: Mfsd1 homozygous and heterozygous mice were born according to the expected Mendelian frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and no differences in weight gain were observed in a longitudinal study in male or female mice between wildtype and Mfsd1 KO mice until 13 weeks-of-age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mfsd1 KO animals have reduced body weight at 12 months of age compared to wildtype animals.
source: However, both male and female Mfsd1 KO animals had a reduced body weight with 12 months-of-age compared to wildtype animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The liver of Mfsd1 KO animals older than 12 weeks shows a tuberous appearance with uneven surface.
source: While young (<10 weeks-of-age) Mfsd1 KO animals were unremarkable, the liver of Mfsd1 KO animals > 12 weeks-of-age revealed a striking pathology characterized by tuberous appearance with uneven surface (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The liver weight normalized to total bodyweight is normal in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: The liver weight (normalized to the total bodyweight) was normal, but the spleen showed a significant increase in size of about twofold (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The spleen shows a significant increase in size of about twofold in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: The liver weight (normalized to the total bodyweight) was normal, but the spleen showed a significant increase in size of about twofold (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) values in serum of Mfsd1 KO mice are significantly elevated.
source: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH) values in serum of Mfsd1 KOs were significantly elevated, but lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and albumin levels were in the normal range, demonstrating established but generally mild damage of the liver parenchyma (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) values in serum of Mfsd1 KO mice are significantly elevated.
source: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH) values in serum of Mfsd1 KOs were significantly elevated, but lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and albumin levels were in the normal range, demonstrating established but generally mild damage of the liver parenchyma (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH) values in serum of Mfsd1 KO mice are significantly elevated.
source: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH) values in serum of Mfsd1 KOs were significantly elevated, but lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and albumin levels were in the normal range, demonstrating established but generally mild damage of the liver parenchyma (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels in serum of Mfsd1 KO mice are in the normal range.
source: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH) values in serum of Mfsd1 KOs were significantly elevated, but lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and albumin levels were in the normal range, demonstrating established but generally mild damage of the liver parenchyma (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Albumin levels in serum of Mfsd1 KO mice are in the normal range.
source: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and glutamate dehydrogenase (GLDH) values in serum of Mfsd1 KOs were significantly elevated, but lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and albumin levels were in the normal range, demonstrating established but generally mild damage of the liver parenchyma (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: No signs of lysosomal storage or abnormal lysosomes are observed at the ultrastructural level in hepatocytes of Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: No signs of lysosomal storage or abnormal lysosomes (enlarged lysosomes, aberrant deposition of abnormal luminal storage compounds) were observed at the ultrastructural level in hepatocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Liver sections of Mfsd1 KO animals at 12 weeks of age show local foci with hepatocyte atrophy or loss.
source: Hematoxylin and eosin and toluidine blue staining of liver sections of Mfsd1 KO animals of 12 weeks-of-age revealed local foci with hepatocyte atrophy or loss.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Ordinary sinusoids in foci of liver damage are absent due to destroyed sinusoidal endothelium in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: Ordinary sinusoids in such foci were absent due to destroyed sinusoidal endothelium.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by histological data in Figure 2H-I.

claim: Wide sinusoids lined by fenestrated endothelium in wildtype mice are replaced by ordinary narrow non-fenestrated capillaries in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: The normally wide sinusoids, which in Mfsd1 wildtype mice were lined by a special fenestrated endothelium (liver sinusoid endothelial cells, LSEC), were in Mfsd1 KO mice replaced by ordinary narrow non-fenestrated capillaries.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2I.

claim: The space of Disse is missing in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: The extravasal space was enlarged and the space of Disse was missing.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by histological data in Figure 2H-I.

claim: Erythrocytes are found in both extra- and intravascular spaces in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: This was indicated by the observation that erythrocytes were found both in extra- and intravasal spaces (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: Sirius Red staining reveals moderate fibrosis in Mfsd1 KO mice, particularly pronounced around focal spots of parenchymal damage.
source: Sirius Red staining revealed moderate fibrosis particularly pronounced around the focal spots of parenchymal damage (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: LSECs are partially absent in spots of focal damage in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: In Mfsd1 KO mice, LSECs were partially absent in spots of focal damage and hepatocytes had direct contact with their microvilli to the blood.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2I.

claim: Platelets are frequently observed at sites of damaged sinusoids in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: Platelets were frequently observed at sites of damaged sinusoids and EM confirmed the increased deposition of collagen and pathologic, non-fenestrated capillaries were observed instead of LSECs (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: CD31 staining is clearly increased in focal spots of liver damage in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: Immunofluorescence staining for CD31, a general marker for endothelial cells, revealed a clearly increased staining in the focal spots of liver damage and confirmed the formation of new capillaries (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2J.

claim: von Willebrand factor (vWF) staining is strikingly increased in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: Staining for von Willebrand factor (vWF), an acute-phase protein that initiates thrombocyte-adhesion and binds the sub-endothelial matrix, was strikingly increased, implicating a pro-thrombotic status of the liver.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2J.

claim: CXCL1 levels are increased in Mfsd1 KO mice as determined by qPCR.
source: The pro-inflammatory and pro-thrombotic conditions were supported by increased levels of CXCL1, MCP1, CD34, MMP2, and MMP9, all markers of inflammation and endothelial remodeling, as determined by qPCR (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2K.

claim: MCP1 levels are increased in Mfsd1 KO mice as determined by qPCR.
source: The pro-inflammatory and pro-thrombotic conditions were supported by increased levels of CXCL1, MCP1, CD34, MMP2, and MMP9, all markers of inflammation and endothelial remodeling, as determined by qPCR (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2K.

claim: CD34 levels are increased in Mfsd1 KO mice as determined by qPCR.
source: The pro-inflammatory and pro-thrombotic conditions were supported by increased levels of CXCL1, MCP1, CD34, MMP2, and MMP9, all markers of inflammation and endothelial remodeling, as determined by qPCR (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2K.

claim: MMP2 levels are increased in Mfsd1 KO mice as determined by qPCR.
source: The pro-inflammatory and pro-thrombotic conditions were supported by increased levels of CXCL1, MCP1, CD34, MMP2, and MMP9, all markers of inflammation and endothelial remodeling, as determined by qPCR (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2K.

claim: MMP9 levels are increased in Mfsd1 KO mice as determined by qPCR.
source: The pro-inflammatory and pro-thrombotic conditions were supported by increased levels of CXCL1, MCP1, CD34, MMP2, and MMP9, all markers of inflammation and endothelial remodeling, as determined by qPCR (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Factor VIII is significantly downregulated in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: Factor VIII, a specific marker for LSECs (Do et al., 1999), was significantly downregulated.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2K, with citation to Do et al., 1999.

claim: Platelets are observed frequently in areas of sinusoidal remodeling in Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: Platelets were observed frequently particularly in areas of sinusoidal remodeling.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Tie2-conditional Mfsd1 knockout mice (Mfsd1flox/flox Tie2 cre) have the same tuberous liver appearance as the full germline Mfsd1 KO.
source: Tie2-conditional mice (Mfsd1flox/flox Tie2 cre) lacked expression of MFSD1 in LSECs but not in hepatocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D), and notably had the same tuberous liver appearance as the full germline Mfsd1 KO, strengthening a pivotal role of MFSD1 in LSECS (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E,F.

claim: A significantly higher occurrence of liver tumors is observed in old Mfsd1 KO animals (>1.5 years).
source: However, we observed a significantly higher occurrence of liver tumors in old animals (>1.5 years), likely as a consequence of fibrosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: GLMP levels are strikingly decreased in isolated liver lysosomes from Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: In confirmation with our proteomics data, GLMP was undetectable in isolated liver lysosomes from Mfsd1 KO mice.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GLMP levels are strongly diminished in all tested tissues of Mfsd1 KO mice including kidney, liver, lung and spleen.
source: GLMP levels were strongly diminished in all tested tissues including kidney, liver, lung and spleen (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: Glmp transcript levels are comparable between wildtype and Mfsd1 KO animals.
source: Notably, qPCR of total liver cDNA revealed comparable levels of the Glmp transcript between wildtype and Mfsd1 KO animals (Figure 3H), indicating a posttranscriptional mechanism leading to GLMP reduction.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3H.

claim: MFSD1 levels are almost completely absent in all analyzed tissues of Glmp KO mice.
source: Immunoblotting of membrane fractions from Glmp KO mice (Kong et al., 2014) revealed an almost complete absence of MFSD1 in all analyzed tissues (brain, heart, kidney, liver, lung and spleen) comparable to the reduction of GLMP in Mfsd1 KO mice (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A, with citation to Kong et al., 2014.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining confirms the absence of immunoreactive MFSD1 in Glmp KO tissue.
source: Immunofluorescence staining of liver and kidney sections additionally confirmed the absence of any immunoreactive MFSD1 in Glmp KO tissue (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mfsd1 transcript levels are unchanged in Glmp KO mice.
source: Similar to the Glmp transcript levels in Mfsd1 KO mice, Mfsd1 transcript levels were unchanged in Glmp KO mice, again pointing towards posttranscriptional regulatory mechanism (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The liver of Glmp KO mice has a tuberous appearance with uneven surface and fibrosis.
source: Interestingly, the liver of Glmp KO mice has, like Mfsd1 KO mice, a tuberous appearance with uneven surface and fibrosis (Kong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to Kong et al., 2014.

claim: Glmp KO mice show local foci where hepatocytes are lost and LSECs are replaced by ordinary capillary endothelium.
source: Similar to Mfsd1 KO mice, Glmp KO mice showed local foci where hepatocytes were lost and LSEC were replaced by ordinary capillary endothelium (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Sites of liver injury in Glmp KO mice show increased staining for CD31 and vWF.
source: Similar to Mfsd1 KO mice, the sites of liver injury in Glmp KO mice showed increased staining for CD31 and vWF at sites of liver injury (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: MFSD1 can be efficiently immunoprecipitated from HeLa cells transfected with HA-tagged GLMP and untagged MFSD1.
source: MFSD1 could be efficiently immunoprecipitated from HeLa cells transfected with HA-tagged GLMP and untagged MFSD1 with the MFSD1-specific antibody and GLMP-HA was co-immunoprecipitated.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: GLMP-HA can be efficiently precipitated with the HA antibody and MFSD1 is co-precipitated.
source: Vice versa, GLMP-HA was efficiently precipitated with the HA antibody and MFSD1 was co-precipitated.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: LAMP1-HA is not co-immunoprecipitated with MFSD1.
source: LAMP1-HA, although expressed with lower efficiency compared to GLMP-HA, included as a negative control, was not co-immunoprecipitated with MFSD1 and not detected even after longer exposure.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The co-immunoprecipitation of MFSD1 and GLMP is highly dependent on the choice of detergent, with CHAPS being effective.
source: It should be noted that the co-immunoprecipitation was highly dependent on the choice of the detergent, and any other tested detergent than CHAPS failed to keep the interaction intact (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FRET is observed between MFSD1 and GLMP fusion proteins.
source: However, notably only the combination of MFSD1 and GLMP, independent of which tag was used, yielded efficient FRET comparable to the positive control of the eGFP-mKATE2 fusion protein, but not any of the negative controls, indicating close proximity of the two proteins and thereby their physical interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GLMP levels are below the limit of detection in Mfsd1 KO MEFs.
source: GLMP levels were below the limit of detection in Mfsd1 KO MEFs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MFSD1 is strongly reduced in Glmp KO MEFs, but not completely absent.
source: MFSD1 on the other hand was strongly reduced in Glmp KO MEFs, but not completely absent as observed before in most murine Glmp KO tissues (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mfsd1 transcript is increased in Glmp KO MEFs.
source: qPCR of MEFs revealed an increase of the transcripts of Mfsd1 in Glmp KO MEFs and an increase of the Glmp transcript in Mfsd1 KO MEFs (Figure 6B), suggesting a transcriptional upregulation as a compensation for the reduced protein levels.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Glmp transcript is increased in Mfsd1 KO MEFs.
source: qPCR of MEFs revealed an increase of the transcripts of Mfsd1 in Glmp KO MEFs and an increase of the Glmp transcript in Mfsd1 KO MEFs (Figure 6B), suggesting a transcriptional upregulation as a compensation for the reduced protein levels.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The remaining amounts of MFSD1 in Glmp KO MEFs do not co-localize with LAMP1, but with the Golgi marker GM130.
source: The remaining amounts of MFSD1 in Glmp KO MEFs notably did not co-localize with LAMP1, but with the Golgi marker GM130.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Transfection of HA-tagged GLMP fully restores the co-localization of MFSD1 with LAMP1 in Glmp KO MEFs.
source: A rescue experiment using transfection of HA-tagged GLMP fully restored the co-localization of MFSD1 with LAMP1 in Glmp KO MEFs, while HA-tagged LAMP1, used as a negative control, did not rescue MFSD1, indicating a critical interdependence of GLMP and MFSD1.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Transfection of HA-tagged MFSD1 in Glmp KO MEFs shows predominantly co-localization with LAMP1.
source: Transfection of HA-tagged MFSD1 in Glmp KO MEFs followed by immunofluorescence staining for HA and LAMP1 revealed predominantly co-localization between MFSD1 and LAMP1, indicating proper sorting to lysosomes (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Expression of HA-tagged GLMP in Mfsd1 KO MEFs shows predominantly lysosomal localization.
source: Vice versa, expression of HA-tagged GLMP in Mfsd1 KO MEFs similarly showed predominantly lysosomal localization.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Treatment with Bafilomycin A partially restores MFSD1 levels in Glmp KO MEFs.
source: Treatment of GLMP wildtype and Glmp KO MEFs with Bafilomycin A (an inhibitor of lysosomal acidification), E64D or Leupeptin (both inhibitors of lysosomal proteases) partially restored the levels of MFSD1 as determined by immunoblot, indicating that accelerated lysosomal proteolysis causes the decrease in MFSD1 levels in the absence of GLMP.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Treatment with E64D partially restores MFSD1 levels in Glmp KO MEFs.
source: Treatment of GLMP wildtype and Glmp KO MEFs with Bafilomycin A (an inhibitor of lysosomal acidification), E64D or Leupeptin (both inhibitors of lysosomal proteases) partially restored the levels of MFSD1 as determined by immunoblot, indicating that accelerated lysosomal proteolysis causes the decrease in MFSD1 levels in the absence of GLMP.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Treatment with Leupeptin partially restores MFSD1 levels in Glmp KO MEFs.
source: Treatment of GLMP wildtype and Glmp KO MEFs with Bafilomycin A (an inhibitor of lysosomal acidification), E64D or Leupeptin (both inhibitors of lysosomal proteases) partially restored the levels of MFSD1 as determined by immunoblot, indicating that accelerated lysosomal proteolysis causes the decrease in MFSD1 levels in the absence of GLMP.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Co-transfection of MFSD1-HA with GLMP significantly reduces the formation of proteolytic fragments.
source: Notably, co-transfection of MFSD1-HA with GLMP, but not LAMP1, significantly reduced the formation of these proteolytic fragments, indicating that specifically GLMP is able to protect MFSD1 from proteolysis (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6G.

claim: GLMP is a highly glycosylated type I transmembrane protein.
source: GLMP is a highly glycosylated type I transmembrane protein previously shown to be a component of the lysosomal membrane (Schieweck et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to Schieweck et al., 2009.

claim: GLMP was previously shown to be a component of the lysosomal membrane.
source: GLMP is a highly glycosylated type I transmembrane protein previously shown to be a component of the lysosomal membrane (Schieweck et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to Schieweck et al., 2009.

claim: MFS transporters move a variety of small compounds across biological membranes.
source: MFS transporters move a variety of small compounds across biological membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: In humans, MFS proteins mediate intestinal nutrient absorption and renal and hepatic clearance.
source: In humans, MFS proteins mediate intestinal nutrient absorption, renal and hepatic clearance, but they have also evolved additional functions in the transport of metabolites and signaling molecules (Quistgaard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the text with citation to Quistgaard et al., 2016.

claim: Lysosomes are major sites for intracellular, acidic hydrolase-mediated proteolysis and cellular degradation.
source: Lysosomes are major sites for intracellular, acidic hydrolase-mediated proteolysis and cellular degradation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract.

claim: The export of low-molecular-weight catabolic end-products from lysosomes is facilitated by polytopic transmembrane proteins.
source: The export of low-molecular-weight catabolic end-products is facilitated by polytopic transmembrane proteins mediating secondary active or passive transport.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract.

claim: MFSD1 is not N-glycosylated, which is unusual for a lysosomal membrane protein.
source: MFSD1 is, unusual for a lysosomal membrane protein, not N-glycosylated.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The phenotype of Mfsd1 KO mice shows similarities to sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS).
source: By comparing the liver and spleen pathology with other pathological situations, especially involving the liver sinusoids, we found some similarities of the phenotype observed in Mfsd1 KO mice (and Glmp KO mice) with 'sinusoidal obstruction syndrome' (SOS), a pathology observed in humans and mouse models treated with oxaliplatin (an adjuvant or neoadjuvant for chemotherapy for colorectal carcinoma) or patients taking pyrrolizidine alkaloid-containing herbal remedies (DeLeve et al., 2002; Fan and Crawford, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to DeLeve et al., 2002 and Fan and Crawford, 2014.

claim: MFSD1 shows relatively high homology to members of the proteobacterial intraphagosomal amino acid transporter (Pht) family.
source: MFSD1 shows a relatively high homology to members of the proteobacterial intraphagosomal amino acid transporter (Pht) family, transporters found in Legionella pneumophila transporting valine and threonine (Sauer et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citation to Sauer et al., 2005.

claim: No major difference in serum amino acid levels is observed between wildtype and Mfsd1 KO mice.
source: However, no major difference for any of the analyzed amino acids was detectable between wildtype and Mfsd1 KO mice in either serum or urine.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A-B.

claim: Direct uptake of radioactively labeled amino acids from acidified cell culture medium in HEK-cells overexpressing MFSD1LL/AA is undetectable.
source: A direct uptake of a radioactively 3H-labeled amino acid mixture, 3H threonine or 3H valine from acidified cell culture medium in HEK-cells overexpressing the MFSD1LL/AA construct was also undetectable (Figure 2—figure supplement 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5C-D.

claim: The interaction between MFSD1 and GLMP differs from the CLC-7/OSTM1 complex in that GLMP and MFSD1 can reach lysosomes independent from each other.
source: However, the interaction between MFSD1 and GLMP differs at least in one regard: GLMP and MFSD1 can reach lysosomes independent from each other, as shown by expression of both proteins in the corresponding KO MEFs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: CLC-7 lacks N-glycosylation.
source: The chloride channel/Cl(-)/H(+)-exchanger CLC-7, similarly lacks N-glycosylation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: OSTM1 stabilizes CLC-7 and is essential for mediating the trafficking of the CLC-7/OSTM1 complex from the ER to lysosomes.
source: Of interest CLC-7 was shown to act in a complex with a single-transmembrane spanning highly glycosylated type I transmembrane protein OSTM1. OSTM1 stabilizes CLC-7 but is also essential for mediating the trafficking of the CLC-7/OSTM1 complex from the ER to lysosomes (Lange et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Lange et al., 2006.

claim: OSTM1 critically regulates Cl(-)/H(+)-exchange.
source: Finally, OSTM1 critically regulates Cl(-)/H(+)-exchange (Leisle et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Leisle et al., 2011.

claim: The correct translocation of MCT-1 critically depends on the interaction with basigin or embigin.
source: The correct translocation of MCT-1, a PM-localized transporter for monocarboxylates such as L-lactate and pyruvate, critically depends on the interaction with basigin or embigin, both highly glycosylated type I transmembrane proteins acting as accessory subunits (Halestrap, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Halestrap, 2012.

claim: Basigin and embigin bear two or three extracellular immunoglobulin domains, respectively.
source: Interestingly, both bear two or three extracellular immunoglobulin domains, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claim: The knockout of ATRAID leads to highly reduced stability of the transporter SLC37A3.
source: Very much like in the situation of MFSD1 and GLMP, the knockout of ATRAID leads to highly reduced stability of the transporter SLC37A3, implicating that ATRAID confers protection to SLC37A3.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with reference to Yu et al., 2018.

claim: SLC37A3 forms a complex with the type I single-transmembrane spanning protein ATRAID.
source: Very recently, another lysosomal SLC-transporter was shown to critically depend on an accessory subunit: the nitrogen-containing-bisphosphonate transporter SLC37A3 forms a complex with the type I single-transmembrane spanning protein ATRAID (all-trans retinoic acid-induced differentiation factor) (Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Yu et al., 2018.

claim: ATRAID has a highly glycosylated luminal N-terminus and a short cytosolic C-terminus.
source: Notably, similar to OSTM1 and GLMP, ATRAID has a highly glycosylated luminal N-terminus and a short cytosolic C-terminus.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion.
